questions.enonce_markdown: What is the name given to rocky bodies that orbit some planets?
questions.corrige_markdown:
A natural satellite (moon) is a rocky (or icy) body held in orbit around a planet by its gravity, for example the Moon around the Earth. Comets are bodies of ice and dust that orbit the Sun, asteroids are rocky bodies that orbit the Sun mainly between Mars and Jupiter, and "planetary bodies" is a general expression that covers planets themselves.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: The planet with the highest surface temperature is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Venus has the hottest surface of all the planets (about 460 to 470 $^\circ$C) because its very dense carbon dioxide atmosphere produces a runaway greenhouse effect. Mercury is closer to the Sun but has almost no atmosphere to retain heat, so its surface is cooler on average.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Below is a diagram (Figure 1) showing the Earth's internal structure (a wedge from the surface O to the centre; depth marks 100 km, 2900 km and 5140 km on the left edge; layers P, Q and R). Use it to answer questions 3, 4 and 5.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

*Figure 1: internal structure of the Earth (layer P between 100 km and 2900 km, layer Q between 2900 km and 5140 km, layer R below 5140 km).*

Which reason below accounts for the solid nature of layer R?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Layer R lies below 5140 km: it is the inner core. Its temperature is very high (several thousand degrees), higher than the melting point of iron-nickel at the surface, yet it is solid. The reason is the enormous pressure at the centre of the Earth, which raises the melting point of the iron alloy above the actual temperature, so that the iron crystallizes. Nickel and iron explain the composition and density, not the physical state, and the inner core is not made of "rocks".

**Answer: B.**

choix.texte: Crystallization of iron due to high pressure.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 1 (the Earth's internal structure, Figure 1: layer P between the 100 km and 2900 km marks, Q between 2900 km and 5140 km, R below 5140 km), also used for questions 3 and 5.

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

What name is given to layer P?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Layer P extends from 100 km down to the 2900 km mark, the core-mantle (Gutenberg) discontinuity. This is the mantle. Layer Q (2900 to 5140 km) is the liquid outer core and R the solid inner core. Among the options, only "Lower Mantle" names a mantle layer; "Crust" and "Oceanic crust" are thin outer layers above P and "Outer core" is layer Q.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Use Figure 1 (the Earth's internal structure, used for questions 3, 4 and 5).

![fig-1](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_1.png)

Which seismic property below best accounts for the physical state of layer Q?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Layer Q is the outer core, which is liquid. A liquid cannot support shear, so S-waves are stopped at the core-mantle boundary, while P-waves (compressional waves) are still transmitted, with a sharp drop in velocity and strong refraction. Of the options, only the transmission of P-waves is a true statement about the outer core: both P and S velocities do not increase through it (options B and D), and S-waves are not refracted through it because they do not pass at all (option C).

**Answer: A.**

choix.texte: Increase in the velocity of both P and S-waves.
Increase in velocity of both P and S-waves.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Earthquake waves in which the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of wave propagation are called:

*Options as printed:* A) Compressional waves   B) Shear waves   C) Longitudinal waves   D) Love waves
questions.corrige_markdown:
In compressional (P) waves, also called longitudinal waves, the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of travel, so options A and C are wrong. In shear (S) waves the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of propagation, which is why they are also called transverse waves. Love waves are surface waves whose horizontal particle motion is also perpendicular to the direction of propagation, so option D is also a defensible answer.

**Intended answer: B (Shear waves).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: They are the most destructive earthquake waves:
questions.corrige_markdown:
L-waves (long or surface waves, Love and Rayleigh waves) travel along the Earth's surface, have the largest amplitude and the longest duration, and cause most of the damage to buildings. P and S waves are body waves of smaller amplitude.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: If a body wave is travelling at 10 km/s, how long will it take to reach the Gutenberg's discontinuity?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Gutenberg discontinuity (core-mantle boundary) lies at a depth of 2900 km (the depth printed on Figure 1). The travel time is $t = \dfrac{d}{v} = \dfrac{2900\ \mathrm{km}}{10\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}} = 290\ \mathrm{s} = 4.83\ \mathrm{min} \approx 5\ \mathrm{min}$.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal drawing below (Figure 2) and answer questions 9, 10 and 11.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: a bipyramidal crystal with its crystallographic axes: a vertical axis labelled +a3 at the top, a horizontal axis +a2 to the right, an axis +a1 at the lower left, a third horizontal axis at the upper left, and the face labelled Y at the lower right.*

How many diagonal planes does the above crystal possess?

*Options as printed:* A) Four   B) Three   C) Seven   D) Six
questions.corrige_markdown:
The crystal is a hexagonal bipyramid (class 6/mmm). Its vertical planes of symmetry fall in two sets: three axial planes (each contains a crystallographic axis) and three diagonal planes (each lies between two axes, at 30 degrees to them). So the crystal has three diagonal planes. Adding the three axial planes and the horizontal plane gives seven planes of symmetry in all.

**Intended answer: B (Three).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal drawing below (Figure 2) and answer questions 9, 10 and 11.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: a bipyramidal crystal with its crystallographic axes: a vertical axis labelled +a3 at the top, a horizontal axis +a2 to the right, an axis +a1 at the lower left, a third horizontal axis at the upper left, and the face labelled Y at the lower right.*

What is the Miller index of the face labelled Y?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The crystal is hexagonal, so the Miller-Bravais index $(h\,k\,i\,l)$ with $h + k + i = 0$ is used. Option B, $(110\bar{1})$, breaks this rule ($1 + 1 + 0 \neq 0$). Face Y is on the lower right: it cuts the $+a_2$ axis (the right-hand vertex), cuts the negative end of the third horizontal axis (the front right vertex), cuts the vertical axis below the centre (the lower apex), and is parallel to $a_1$. The intercepts are therefore $a_1 = \infty$, $a_2 = 1$, $a_3 = -1$, $c = -1$, and the reciprocals give $(0\,1\,\bar{1}\,\bar{1})$. Check: $0 + 1 - 1 = 0$. Options A and D are the faces parallel to $a_2$ (upper and lower), so they are not face Y.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the crystal drawing below (Figure 2) and answer questions 9, 10 and 11.

![fig-2](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_2.png)

*Figure 2: a bipyramidal crystal with its crystallographic axes: a vertical axis labelled +a3 at the top, a horizontal axis +a2 to the right, an axis +a1 at the lower left, a third horizontal axis at the upper left, and the face labelled Y at the lower right.*

The most appropriate name of the form shown by the crystal above is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The form has two apices (top and bottom) joined to a six-sided equator, so it is a hexagonal bipyramid, not a prism (which has parallel vertical faces and no apex). The crystallographic axes emerge through the equatorial corners of the crystal (the edges), not through the middle of faces: this is the first-order position, the form $\{10\bar{1}1\}$. In a second-order bipyramid the axes would emerge through the middle of the faces. The most complete name is therefore hexagonal bipyramid of first order.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Hexagonal prism of the second order.

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagrams below (Figure 3) represent structures of some silicate minerals (Structure N: a single row of linked tetrahedra; Structure M: two rows of linked tetrahedra). Study and answer questions 12, 13 and 14.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: silicate structures N (single chain of SiO4 tetrahedra) and M (double chain of SiO4 tetrahedra).*

A mineral that possesses the structure labelled N is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Structure N is a single chain of SiO4 tetrahedra, each tetrahedron sharing two oxygen atoms with its neighbours (ratio Si:O = 1:3). This is the structure of the pyroxene group, to which augite belongs. Hornblende (amphibole) has a double chain, biotite a sheet structure and olivine isolated tetrahedra.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagrams below (Figure 3) represent structures of some silicate minerals (Structure N: a single row of linked tetrahedra; Structure M: two rows of linked tetrahedra). Study and answer questions 12, 13 and 14.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: silicate structures N (single chain of SiO4 tetrahedra) and M (double chain of SiO4 tetrahedra).*

The silicon-oxygen ratio of the structure labelled M is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Structure M is a double chain (the amphibole structure, for example hornblende). In a double chain half of the tetrahedra share two oxygen atoms and half share three, so on average each tetrahedron has 2.75 oxygen atoms of its own: the repeating unit is $\mathrm{Si_4O_{11}}$, ratio Si:O = 4:11. Ratio 1:4 is for isolated tetrahedra (olivine) and 2:5 for sheets.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagrams below (Figure 3) represent structures of some silicate minerals (Structure N: a single row of linked tetrahedra; Structure M: two rows of linked tetrahedra). Study and answer questions 12, 13 and 14.

![fig-3](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_3.png)

*Figure 3: silicate structures N (single chain of SiO4 tetrahedra) and M (double chain of SiO4 tetrahedra).*

What is the difference between structures M and N?
questions.corrige_markdown:
N is a single chain: every tetrahedron shares two corner oxygen atoms. M is a double chain: two single chains are cross-linked, so alternate tetrahedra share two and three oxygen atoms. Option A describes an island silicate (olivine), option B calls M a sheet (it is a double chain, not a sheet), and option D confuses the cation linkage (Fe and Mg bond between chains) with the sharing of oxygen atoms.

**Answer: C.**

choix.texte: Structure M has separate $\mathrm{SiO_4}$ tetrahedra while structure N is linked.
Structure M has a sheet structure while structure N has a chain structure.
In M, each tetrahedron shares two and three oxygen atoms while in N only two oxygen atoms are shared.
In structure M, each tetrahedron is linked by $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ while in N each tetrahedron shares three atoms with its neighbours.

Which of the following rock types represented by the letters W, X, Y and Z would be the last to crystallize from a primary magma?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Bowen's reaction series the first minerals to crystallize are the dark, silica-poor minerals (olivine, calcium-rich plagioclase) and the last are the silica-rich ones (sodium-rich plagioclase, K-feldspar, muscovite and quartz). The most silica-rich composition is W (70.6 per cent $\mathrm{SiO_2}$, acid, granite or rhyolite type), so W crystallizes last, while Y (ultrabasic) crystallizes first.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A metamorphic rock rich in garnet and pyroxene formed at extremely high pressure and temperature around mountain belts is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Eclogite is the very high-pressure, high-temperature metamorphic rock of basaltic composition, made of red garnet (pyrope-almandine) and green sodium-rich pyroxene (omphacite); it forms in subduction zones and deep in mountain belts. Amphibolite is rich in hornblende and plagioclase, granulite forms at high temperature and moderate pressure, and hornfels forms at low pressure by contact metamorphism.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Hornfels, a non-foliated metamorphic rock, has the following textures:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Hornfels is a contact-metamorphic rock formed by heating without directed pressure, so its grains recrystallize into an interlocking mosaic of grains of about the same shape and size in all directions: the texture is granoblastic and the grains are equidimensional. Porphyroblastic means large crystals set in a finer matrix, and an inequidimensional texture is typical of foliated (schistose or gneissic) rocks.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: An index mineral formed at the highest metamorphic grade is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
In Barrow's regional metamorphic zones of pelitic rocks the index minerals appear in the order chlorite, biotite, garnet, staurolite, kyanite and sillimanite as the grade rises. Sillimanite marks the highest grade of the four options, while chlorite marks the lowest.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 4) shows a fold truncated by a fault (F-F). Use it to answer questions 21 and 22.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: geological map of beds a, b, c and d, with a dip of 50 degrees (arrow pointing south-west) on the left, a dip of 20 degrees (arrow pointing east-north-east) on the right, the fault F-F and a north arrow.*

Identify the type of fold.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The beds strike north-west to south-east. On the left the bed dips at 50 degrees towards the south-west and on the right the bed dips at 20 degrees towards the north-east: the two limbs dip away from each other, so the fold is arch-shaped (an antiform), with the oldest unit d in the core. A fold that is arched with the older beds in the core is an anticline (an asymmetrical one, since the dips are 50 and 20 degrees). A syncline or synform would have limbs dipping towards each other, and an antiformal syncline would have the younger beds in the core of an arch.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 4) shows a fold truncated by a fault (F-F). Use it to answer questions 21 and 22.

![fig-4](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_4.png)

*Figure 4: geological map of beds a, b, c and d, with a dip of 50 degrees (arrow pointing south-west) on the left, a dip of 20 degrees (arrow pointing east-north-east) on the right, the fault F-F and a north arrow.*

State the trend of the fold.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The trend of a fold is the direction of its axis, which is parallel to the strike of the beds. The bed boundaries run from the upper left to the lower right of the map, that is from north-west to south-east (the north arrow points up). The dips are measured at right angles to this, towards the south-west and the north-east. The trend is NW-SE.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A vein of sapphire in Mbiame (Banso) dips towards the NE direction. What will be the strike of that bed?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Strike is the direction of a horizontal line on the surface of the bed, and it is always at right angles to the direction of dip. The bed dips to the north-east (bearing 045 degrees), so the strike is at 90 degrees to it, along 315 and 135 degrees: NW-SE.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What stage of a river is characterized by a high erosive power?
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the youthful (upper) stage the river has a steep gradient, a high velocity and cuts down vertically, forming V-shaped valleys, rapids and waterfalls: its erosive power is highest. In the mature and old stages the gradient is gentler and lateral erosion and deposition become more important.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 5) represents a feature produced by aeolian erosion (alternating bands of hard rock and soft rock, with long ridges separated by troughs). Study the diagram and answer questions 25 and 26.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: a rock surface of alternating hard and soft rock bands eroded by wind into long parallel ridges and troughs.*

Identify the feature on the diagram above.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The diagram shows long, parallel ridges of resistant (hard) rock separated by troughs cut in the weaker (soft) rock bands, all aligned with the direction of the prevailing wind. These streamlined ridges are yardangs. Zeugen are tabular masses with a hard cap over soft rock, deflation hollows are basins hollowed by the removal of loose material, and ventifacts are individual stones polished and faceted by wind-blown sand.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The diagram below (Figure 5) represents a feature produced by aeolian erosion (alternating bands of hard rock and soft rock, with long ridges separated by troughs). Study the diagram and answer questions 25 and 26.

![fig-5](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_5.png)

*Figure 5: a rock surface of alternating hard and soft rock bands eroded by wind into long parallel ridges and troughs.*

The main erosional process that led to the formation of the feature above is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Yardangs are cut mainly by corrasion (abrasion): wind-blown sand and dust grind the rock surface, and the soft rock bands are worn away faster than the hard bands, leaving ridges. Deflation only removes loose material, attrition is the wearing of the transported particles themselves, and corrosion is chemical solution, which is not the main process in a desert.

**Answer: D.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A sandstone with more than 15% fine grained matrix of mud, silt and clay together with quartz, feldspar and rock fragments is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A sandstone with more than 15 per cent of fine matrix and a mixture of quartz, feldspar and rock fragments is a greywacke (wacke). Quartz arenite and orthoquartzite are clean, well sorted quartz sandstones with little matrix (less than 5 per cent), and arkose is a sandstone with more than 25 per cent feldspar and little matrix.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:

The cumulative curve labelled C indicates that the sediment is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
On a cumulative frequency curve the steeper the curve, the narrower the range of grain sizes: almost all the grains of sample C fall in a very narrow size range, shown by its near-vertical rise from about 5 per cent to 100 per cent over a small change of particle size. This is a well-sorted sediment (for example a beach or dune sand). A gently sloping curve such as B or A indicates a poorly sorted sediment.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the cumulative frequency curves below (Figure 6) and answer questions 28 and 29.

![fig-6](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_6.png)

*Figure 6: cumulative frequency curves A, B and C (cumulative per cent from 0 to 100 against particle size from 8 to 1/32); curve C is very steep between sizes 2 and 1/2, curve B rises gradually and reaches about 95 per cent, curve A starts at 25 per cent, is almost flat and rises to about 60 per cent at size 1/16.*

What is the most common structure displayed by sediments represented by curve A?

*Options as printed:* A) Cross bedding   B) Ripple marks   C) Graded bedding   D) Slump structures
questions.corrige_markdown:
Curve A is almost flat over most of its length, so the sample holds a very wide range of grain sizes (gravel to fine silt) and is poorly sorted. Of the structures listed, graded bedding is the one that is made of poorly sorted sediment, with coarse grains at the base passing upwards to fine grains. Cross bedding and ripple marks are typical of well-sorted sands such as curve C, while slump structures are deformation structures rather than depositional ones.

**Intended answer: C (Graded bedding).**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following index fossils is common in Ordovician shale?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Graptolites are the characteristic index fossils of Ordovician (and Silurian) black shales: they evolved quickly, floated widely and are found in fine-grained marine mud. Micraster is a Cretaceous echinoid and ammonites are Mesozoic. Trilobites occur in the Ordovician, but they are best known as the index fossil of the Cambrian.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 7), which shows the shape of a fossil. Use it to answer questions 31 and 32.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Figure 7: a graptolite colony hanging down from a point at the top, with four serrated branches; X is the outer branch and Y marks the serrated edge of a branch.*

Identify the features labelled X and Y respectively:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Figure 7 is a graptolite colony (rhabdosome). The branches that radiate from the sicula are the stipes, so X, which points to a branch, is a stipe. The small cup-shaped serrations along each stipe, which housed the individual zooids, are the thecae, which Y indicates. The nema and sicula are at the apex (the thin spine at the top), and the rhabdosome is the whole colony.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the diagram below (Figure 7), which shows the shape of a fossil. Use it to answer questions 31 and 32.

![fig-7](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_7.png)

*Figure 7: a graptolite colony hanging down from a point at the top, with four serrated branches; X is the outer branch and Y marks the serrated edge of a branch.*

The orientation of the stipes above can be best described as:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The four stipes hang downwards from the sicula, nearly parallel to each other, with the apex at the top: this orientation is called pendent. Scandent stipes grow upwards, reclined stipes sag slightly below the horizontal and declined stipes droop below the horizontal at a wider angle.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the following radioactive isotope has the longest half-life?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The half-lives are about 1.25 billion years for potassium-40, 4.47 billion years for uranium-238, 14 billion years for thorium-232 and about 48.8 billion years for rubidium-87. Rubidium-87 has the longest half-life, so the rubidium-strontium method is used for very old rocks.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A feldspathic sandstone is dated using the potassium-argon method. The date obtained will indicate when the:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A sandstone is made of grains of older rocks. The potassium-argon clock in a feldspar grain started when that crystal formed and cooled below its closing temperature in its parent igneous or metamorphic rock, long before the grain was deposited as sediment. The date therefore gives the age of the feldspar crystal, not the age of the sandstone.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: A radioactive element undergoes decay to produce a stable daughter product. The half-life of this decay process is 3 million years. Determine the percentage of the daughter produced after a period of 9 million years.
questions.corrige_markdown:
The number of half-lives is $n = \dfrac{9}{3} = 3$. The fraction of parent left is $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{1}{8} = 12.5\%$, so the fraction of daughter produced is $100\% - 12.5\% = 87.5\%$, which is option C (87%, the nearest of the options). Option A is the percentage of parent remaining, and 13.5% is not a result of this decay.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the map below (Figure 8) and answer questions 36 and 37.

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: geological map with north arrow: bed boundaries on the left form nested closures around the core bed P that point east, a vertical strip J-H separates the two halves, and the bed boundaries on the right are curves that close towards the east (letters a, b, c, d, M, O, S mark beds and points).*

The core bed P is older. Name the type of fold.
questions.corrige_markdown:
In the map the outcrop of the beds is folded into nested U-shaped patterns around the core bed P. When the bed in the core of a fold is the oldest, with progressively younger beds outwards, the fold is an anticline. In a syncline the core is the youngest bed, and the terms antiform and synform describe the shape only, when the ages are not known; here the age is given, so anticline is the correct name.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Study the map below (Figure 8) and answer questions 36 and 37.

![fig-8](gce-al-geology-2024-p1-officiel-cameroun_exercice_1_fig_8.png)

*Figure 8: geological map with north arrow: bed boundaries on the left form nested closures around the core bed P that point east, a vertical strip J-H separates the two halves, and the bed boundaries on the right are curves that close towards the east (letters a, b, c, d, M, O, S mark beds and points).*

What is the plunge direction of the fold?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The outcrop pattern of a plunging anticline forms a V or U shape that closes in the direction of plunge, because the fold axis dips below the surface in that direction and the older core beds disappear. On the map the nested closures around bed P close towards the east (the right side of the map; north is up), so the fold plunges to the east.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What major feature is formed during the convergence of two oceanic plates?
questions.corrige_markdown:
When two oceanic plates converge, the older, denser plate is subducted beneath the other and a deep oceanic trench forms at the line of subduction (with a volcanic island arc on the overriding plate). Fold mountains form when continental plates collide, ridges form at divergent boundaries and hot spots are not plate-boundary features.

**Answer: D.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: A chaotically mixed and deformed rock associated with convergent plate boundaries is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
A melange is a chaotic mixture of blocks of different rocks (greywacke, chert, basalt, serpentinite and others) in a sheared matrix, formed in subduction zones where the accretionary wedge is deformed. Blueschist is a metamorphic rock of high pressure and low temperature, turbidite is a sediment deposited by turbidity currents, and an ophiolite is a slice of oceanic crust and mantle emplaced on land.

**Answer: A.**
themes: plate tectonics and sea floor spreading

questions.enonce_markdown: Grains of gold were washed from a heavy stream sediment. Under what type of mineral deposit will it be classified?
questions.corrige_markdown:
Gold is dense and chemically resistant, so it is concentrated as grains by running water in stream gravels and sands: this is a detrital (placer) mineral deposit. Secondary and supergene enrichment deposits form by the downward leaching and re-deposition of metals in a sulphide ore body, and residual deposits are formed in place by weathering.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
A type of mineral deposit formed when mineralized solutions invade a limestone host rock is:

*Options as printed:* A) Pyrometasomatic deposit   B) Pneumatolytic deposit   C) Hydrothermal depoit   D) Pegmatite deposit
questions.corrige_markdown:
Limestone is chemically reactive: hot mineralized solutions given off by an intrusion replace the carbonate rock at the contact and form skarn bodies of garnet, epidote, magnetite and sulphides. This is the pyrometasomatic (contact metasomatic) type of deposit. Hydrothermal deposits can also replace limestone, so the printed options are not entirely exclusive.

**Intended answer: A (Pyrometasomatic deposit).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: A deposit which is worked because it contains some valuable elements is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
An ore deposit is a mineral deposit that contains one or more valuable elements in a concentration high enough to be worked at a profit. A mineral deposit is any natural concentration of a mineral, even if it is not economic, and an ore body is the mass of ore itself within a deposit.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Two examples of dimension stones are:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Dimension stones are rocks quarried in blocks of a specified size and shape for building and monuments: granite (for facing and paving) and limestone (for walls and cladding) are standard examples. Shale is too weak and fissile to be cut into blocks, and the pairs given in options B, C and D each include at least one rock that is not a typical dimension stone.

**Answer: A.**
themes: engineering geology and quarry site selection

questions.enonce_markdown: An example of surface mining is:
questions.corrige_markdown:
Surface mining removes the overburden and works the ore from the surface in open pits, quarries and strips: strip mining is a surface method. Room and pillar mining and tunnelling are underground methods, and artisanal mining describes the scale of the operation, not a mining method.

**Answer: B.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
The most effective approach of minimizing the impacts of landslides is to:

*Options as printed:* A) Construct retaining walls   B) Plant vegetation on slopes   C) Educate and advice the population   D) Terracing the slopes
questions.corrige_markdown:
Engineering methods (retaining walls, terracing) and biological methods (vegetation) reduce the risk at a particular slope, but they are costly or local. Educating the population on the signs of instability and on avoiding construction on unstable slopes reduces losses everywhere and is generally put forward as the most effective way to lessen the impacts of landslides.

**Intended answer: C (Educate and advice the population).**

The printed question is not reliable enough to be marked automatically so it is left open for self-assessment instead of being auto-marked.

questions.enonce_markdown: The climatic change as a result of an increase in the world's temperature is called:
questions.corrige_markdown:
The rise in the average temperature of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans that causes climatic change is called global warming. The greenhouse effect is the mechanism (heat trapped by gases such as carbon dioxide and methane) that causes it, and climatic variability is natural variation of climate over time.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: Which formations below constitute the source and reservoir rocks of the Rio del Rey basin in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The Rio del Rey basin is the Cameroonian part of the Niger Delta system and has the same stratigraphy: the Akata Formation (prodelta marine shales) is the source rock and the Agbada Formation (alternating deltaic sandstones and shales) is the main reservoir. Mundeck, Logbajeck, Souellaba and Nkappa are formations of the Douala basin.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown: What is the age range of sedimentary rocks in Cameroon?
questions.corrige_markdown:
The sedimentary basins of Cameroon (the coastal Douala and Rio del Rey basins, the Benue trough and the Garoua basin, and the Lake Chad basin) are filled mainly with Cretaceous to Tertiary sediments (about 140 to 2 million years old). Option C is the range that covers the main basins; the Quaternary alluvium is superficial.

**Answer: C.**

questions.enonce_markdown: During the crystallization of magma, at what stage is the magma characterized by a silica-rich phase and volatiles such as HCl, HF, CO2, H2O and H2S?
questions.corrige_markdown:
After most of the magma has crystallized, the residual melt is enriched in silica, alkalis and volatile components (water, carbon dioxide, hydrogen chloride, hydrogen fluoride, hydrogen sulphide). Crystallization from this volatile-rich silica melt forms pegmatites with very large crystals: this is the pegmatitic stage. In the following pneumatolytic stage the volatiles escape as gases, and in the hydrothermal stage hot aqueous solutions deposit minerals in veins.

**Answer: A.**

questions.enonce_markdown:
Which of the following type of eruption is the most explosive?

*Options as printed:* A) Pelean type   B) Vesuvian type   C) Krakatoan type   D) Strombolian type
questions.corrige_markdown:
Eruption types in order of increasing violence are Hawaiian, Strombolian, Vulcanian, Vesuvian and Pelean, and the most violent of all is the Krakatoan type, a catastrophic eruption in which the volcano blows itself apart and a caldera collapses (Krakatoa, 1883). Strombolian eruptions are mild and rhythmic.

**Intended answer: C (Krakatoan type).**
